text:
“But I assure you,” I added in a cold tone, as though I had wished to prove that I was forever cured of my passion, “I assure you that I am not angry. It was perfectly natural that someone should be waiting for you, just as it is perfectly natural for me to leave at three in the morning.”

“Do you also have someone waiting for you at home?”

“No, but I must go.”

“Goodbye, then.”

“You are sending me away?”

“Not in the least.”

“Why are you hurting me?”

“How have I hurt you?”

“You tell me that someone was waiting for you.”

“I could not help laughing at the thought that you had been so happy to see me come home alone, when there was such a good reason for it.”

“One often takes childish delight in a trifle, and it is cruel to destroy that delight when, by allowing it to remain, one can make the person who finds it happier still.”

“But whom do you think you are dealing with? I am neither a virgin nor a duchess. I have known you only since today, and I owe you no account of my actions. Even supposing that one day I become your mistress, you must understand clearly that I have had other lovers besides you. If you are already making jealous scenes before it happens, what will it be like afterward, if there ever is an afterward! I have never seen a man like you.”

“That is because no one has ever loved you as I love you.”

“Come now, honestly, do you really love me so much?”

“As much as it is possible to love, I believe.”

“And this has been going on since...?”

“Since a day when I saw you step down from a carriage and enter Susse’s, three years ago.”

“Do you know that is very beautiful? Well then, what must I do to acknowledge this great love?”

“You must love me a little,” I said, with a pounding heart that almost prevented me from speaking; for, despite the half-mocking smiles with which she had accompanied this entire conversation, it seemed to me that Marguerite was beginning to share my agitation, and that I was approaching the hour I had awaited for so long.

“Well, and the duke?”

“What duke?”

“My jealous old man.”

“He will know nothing about it.”

“And if he does find out?”

“He will forgive you.”

“Oh, no! He will abandon me, and what will become of me?”

“You certainly risk his abandoning you for another man.”

“How do you know?”

“From the instruction you gave that no one was to be admitted tonight.”

“That is true; but that man is a serious lover.”

“One for whom you care very little, since you have your door barred to him at such an hour.”

“You are hardly the person to reproach me for that, since it was in order to receive you, you and your friend.”

Little by little I had moved closer to Marguerite; I had put my hands around her waist, and I could feel her supple body resting lightly upon my clasped hands.

“If you only knew how I love you!” I said to her softly.

“Is that really true?”

“I swear it to you.”

“Well, if you promise to do everything I wish without saying a word, without raising an objection, without questioning me, I may love you.”

“Anything you wish!”

“But I warn you: I want to be free to do whatever I please, without giving you the slightest detail about my life. For a long time I have been looking for a young lover, with no will of his own, loving without suspicion, loved without rights. I have never been able to find one. Men, instead of being satisfied that one grants them for a long time what they would scarcely have hoped to obtain once, demand from their mistress an account of the present, the past, and even the future. As they grow accustomed to her, they want to dominate her, and they become all the more demanding the more one gives them everything they want. If I decide to take a new lover now, I want him to possess three very rare qualities: I want him to be trusting, submissive, and discreet.”

“Well, I shall be anything you wish.”

“We shall see.”

“And when shall we see?”

“Later.”

“Why?”

“Because,” said Marguerite, freeing herself from my arms and taking from a large bouquet of red camellias brought that morning a camellia which she placed in my buttonhole, “because treaties cannot always be carried out on the day they are signed. It is easy to understand.”

“And when shall I see you again?” I said, pressing her in my arms.

“When this camellia changes color.”

“And when will it change color?”

“Tomorrow, from eleven until midnight. Are you satisfied?”

“You ask me that?”

“Not a word about any of this to your friend, or to Prudence, or to anyone at all.”

“I promise you.”

“Now kiss me, and let us go back into the dining room.”

She offered me her lips, smoothed her hair once more, and we left that room, she singing, I half mad.

In the drawing room she stopped and said softly to me:

“It must seem strange to you that I appear ready to accept you like this, at once; do you know what causes it? It is because,” she continued, taking my hand and placing it against her heart, whose violent, repeated throbbing I felt, “it is because, as I am destined to live less long than others, I have promised myself to live more quickly.”

“Do not speak to me like that again, I beg you.”

“Oh! Take comfort,” she continued, laughing. “However little time I may have to live, I shall live longer than you will love me.”

And she went into the dining room singing.

“Where is Nanine?” she said when she saw Gaston and Prudence alone.

“She is asleep in your bedroom, waiting for you to go to bed,” Prudence replied.

“The poor creature! I am killing her! Come, gentlemen, be off; it is time.”

Ten minutes later, Gaston and I went out. Marguerite squeezed my hand as she said goodbye to me and remained with Prudence.

“Well,” Gaston asked me when we were outside, “what do you say of Marguerite?”

“She is an angel, and I am mad about her.”

“I suspected as much; did you tell her?”

“Yes.”

“And did she promise to believe you?”

“No.”

“That is not how it was with Prudence.”

“She promised you?”

“She did better than that, my dear fellow! One would never believe it, but that fat Duvernoy is still very fine!”
